citations.cited_for: NC TSPA may preempt unjust enrichment and/or civil conspiracy claims based solely on trade secret misappropriation
citations.context: the NC Trade Secrets Protection Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. § 66-157(a)) may preempt the unjust enrichment and/or civil conspiracy claims insofar as they are based solely on trade secret misappropriation

first_check.correct_citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 66-157 (statute of limitations; it has no subsection (a))
first_check.explanation: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 66-157 has no subsection (a). The section is one sentence setting the 3-year limitations period, and it says nothing about preemption. No section of the NC Trade Secrets Protection Act (§§ 66-152 to 66-157) contains a preemption or displacement clause like the one in the Uniform Trade Secrets Act. So the cited provision cannot support the claim that the Act may preempt unjust enrichment or civil conspiracy claims. Any such argument would have to come from case law, not from § 66-157(a).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: G.S. 66-157. Statute of limitations. An action for misappropriation of a trade secret must be commenced within three years after the misappropriation complained of is or reasonably should have been discovered.

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The citation appears in the task.json rubric (ISSUE_008), which says the NC Trade Secrets Protection Act, cited as "N.C. Gen. Stat. § 66-157(a)", may preempt the unjust enrichment and civil conspiracy claims. I read the official NC General Assembly text of Article 24 (§§ 66-152 to 66-157). § 66-157 has no subsections. It is one sentence titled "Statute of limitations": "An action for misappropriation of a trade secret must be commenced within three years after the misappropriation complained of is or reasonably should have been discovered." I searched the full article text for "preempt", "displace", "exclusive", "supersede" and "other remed". None of those terms appears. No section has a UTSA-style displacement clause; §§ 66-158 through 66-162 are "Reserved for future codification purposes." The only nearby language is in § 66-155, which says the section "shall not be construed to deprive the person against whom relief is sought of any other defenses provided under the law." That is about defenses, not preemption. So the statute is real but does not support the preemption proposition, and the pinpoint "(a)" does not exist. MISCHARACTERIZED is the right status. The wrong subsection is a secondary defect.
